props.title: Der Golem
props.initialSlug: Jewish folklore brought to life with expressionist style

sections.content: **Der Golem** (1920) stands as a towering achievement of German Expressionist horror, alongside **The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari** (1920) and **Nosferatu** (1922). Director Paul Wegener's third and final Golem film draws from Jewish folklore to tell the story of a clay creature awakened to protect Prague's Jewish ghetto. The film's incredible set design by architect Hans Poelzig creates a twisted, angular world of cramped streets and looming buildings that influenced horror cinema for decades, directly inspiring later works like **Frankenstein** (1931) and **The Bride of Frankenstein** (1935).

sections.content: The film's influence on monster movies cannot be overstated. The Golem's design and Paul Wegener's performance as the clay creature established many tropes that would define sympathetic movie monsters. The creature's struggle with its own existence and power directly influenced James Whale's approach to **Frankenstein** (1931), while the religious and mystical elements echo through films like **The Dybbuk** (1937) and much later in **Angels in America** (2003).

The technical achievements of **Der Golem** (1920) were revolutionary for their time. Karl Freund's cinematography utilized innovative lighting techniques that would become hallmarks of horror cinema. The film's practical effects, particularly in bringing the Golem to life through the placement of the magical amulet, influenced special effects in fantasy films for generations, seen in works like **Jason and the Argonauts** (1963) and even **The Terminator** (1984). movies.title: Frankenstein
movies.slug: James Whale's iconic adaptation of Mary Shelley's novel, featuring Boris Karloff as the monster. Heavily influenced by Der Golem.

sections.content: **Der Golem** (1920) remains one of the earliest and most significant representations of Jewish mythology in cinema. Its exploration of the Golem legend opened doors for other films drawing from Jewish folklore, from **The Dybbuk** (1937) to modern interpretations like **A Serious Man** (2009) and **Pi** (1998). The film's themes of protection, power, and the dangerous allure of forbidden knowledge continue to resonate.
